Groups of animals

Among the larger groups of animals now recognize~ by science, the one known as the
Chordata is naturally the most familiar Including the mammals, birds, reptiles and fishes,
besides numerous forms less well known Another group, also familiar, called the Mollusca,
includes the snails, clams, etc The starfish and sea urchin, often seen at the seashore, belong
with other similar animals to a third group called the Echinodermata A multitude of tiny beings,
almost all too small to be seen without the aid of a microscope, are included 'in the group
Protozoa A fifth large group is composed mainly of soft, jellylike animals, the more common
larger members being called jellyfish, and to this group the name Coelenterata is applied.

Several other groups including various kinds of worms and less familiar forms are also known
Arthropoda

The largest group of all, however, is the Arthropoda

Its members found in the seas, in fresh water, on land or even flying freely

A group with remarkable differences of structure, and so abundant that all the other animals
taken together are less than one-sixth as many as the arthropods

Well-known members of this group are

The lobsters, cray fish and crabs

Scorpions, spiders, mites, ticks

The centipedes and millipedes

Last, and most abundant of all, the insects

2-Characteristics of Arthropod
No one feature will serve to separate the arthropods from' all other animals

But the possession by an animal of several of those here described will enable the observer to
determine in each case whether he is examining one of this group.

In arthropods the body is composed of a series of more or less similar pieces or segments

Placed one behind another, the line of attachment of these to each other being usually
somewhat evident on parts of the body at least

This character is also shown, and indeed more clearly, in some
worms, such as the common earthworm Another character of the
arthropods is the presence of jointed legs (or appendages of some
kind), as is indicated by the name of the group, and these are not
possessed by worms

The surface of the body is covered by a secretion which hardens
on exposure to the air, forming an outside shell or external skeleton
called exoskeleton

   1. Enlist the insects that used as human food.
Man in some parts of the world consumes large quantities of grasshoppers, crickets, ants and other
insects.
The great value of some insects and the great losses, sometimes enormous, caused by others make it
obviously important to encourage the beneficial forms while striving to prevent or at least to reduce
the losses caused by the injurious ones
   2. Cultural method
Cultural control focuses on changing the environment to make it less favorable for insects. This can
include practices like crop rotation, planting resistant varieties, and adjusting irrigation and
fertilization to reduce pest habitat.
   3. Why pests brought in our country?
Pests can be brought into a country through various means such as international trade, travel, or even
natural migration. Sometimes, pests can hitch a ride on imported goods, plants, or animals. They can
also spread through wind, water, or by simply moving from one place to another. It’s important for
countries to have strict regulations and quarantine measures to prevent the introduction and spread
of invasive pests.
   4. What is coxa?
The coxa is the segment that articulates with the body, frequently partly lying in a more or less cup
shaped hollow of the latter. It may be short or long and is generally freely movable on the body and
powerful. This arrangement allows for movement and flexibility.
   5. Integrated pest management?
Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is an approach that focuses on using a combination of techniques
to manage pests in a sustainable and environmentally-friendly way. It involves strategies like
biological control, cultural practices, and targeted pesticide use, all while minimizing harm to
beneficial organisms and the environment. IPM aims to reduce reliance on chemical pesticides and
promote long-term pest management. It’s a great approach for maintaining healthy plants and
ecosystems.

                             SHORT QUESTIONS(3)
   1)    Name the parts of legs in insects?
Legs of insects (adults and larvae) are jointed and have five parts:
   1) coxa,
   2) trochanter,
   3) femur,
   4) tibia, and
   5) tarsus.
   2)    Name the part of head of insects/Structures of head?
Structures found on the head are
   1) A pair of antennae
   2) Two compound eyes (ocelli)
   3) The mouth parts

   3)    Define Cerci?
A pair of many-segmented, antenna-like structures, sometimes short, sometimes long,
may occur at the end of the abdomen. And these are called cerci. They probably serve
as organs of touch and possibly organ of smell in some cases.
   4)    What is coxa in insects?
The coxa is the segment that articulates with the body, frequently partly lying in a more
or less cup shaped hollow of the latter. It may be short or long and is generally freely
movable on the body and powerful. This arrangement allows for movement and
flexibility.
   5)    What are tracheal gills?
Insects that live in water during their early stages of life cannot breathe air into their
bodies through spiracles like they do when they are on land. Instead, they have special
structures called tracheal gills that allow them to obtain oxygen from the water. These
tracheal gills help them breathe while they’re in the water.
   6)    What is meant by contact insecticides?
It was formerly supposed that certain materials called contact insecticides, which kill
insects by contact with their bodies. They caused death by entering the spiracles and
closing them up, thus producing suffocation.
   7)    Define Ovipositor?
The ovipositor is a combination of different parts at the end of the abdomen in female
insects that lay their eggs inside objects. It helps them make a hole or slit in the object
and guide the eggs into it. It usually consists of about three pairs of parts, which can be
long or short, slender or stout, depending on the insect. In some insects, the ovipositor
has transformed into a sting because they no longer need to make holes for egg laying.
   8)    How skeleton is formed in Arthropoda?

In arthropods, the skeleton is formed by a process called ecdysis or molting. When an
arthropod grows, its exoskeleton becomes too small and rigid. To accommodate
growth, the arthropod sheds its old exoskeleton and forms a new one. This process
allows them to renew and replace their skeleton as they continue to grow. The surface
of the body is covered by a secretion which hardens on exposure to the air, forming an
outside new shell or external skeleton called exoskeleton.
   9)    Differentiate between Pulivillus, Pulvilli, And Epodium ?
Pulivillus: a soft, padlike structure located at the base of each claw on the feet of
certain insects.
Pulvilli: Pulvilli are lobes or pads that are located between the tarsal claws of many
insects.
Empodium: Between the pulvilli there is often a spine that is called the empodium.
   10) Differentiate between exoskeleton of Arthropoda and
       Molluska/How form exoskeleton of insects?
Both mollusks and arthropods have an external skeleton, which gives them a shell-like
appearance. However, the materials that make up their skeletons are different.
   • Mollusks have a skeleton made mostly of calcium carbonate. e.g. snails.
   • While arthropods have a skeleton made of chitin, which is similar to horn.
     Sometimes, arthropods also have calcareous salts deposited in their chitin. e.g.
     spiders and insects.

In the Hemimetabola, then the stages of life are
   1) Egg
   2) Nymph
   3) Adult
Found in In three of the orders: (from handout)
   1) Ephemerida (mayflies)
   2) Odonata (dragonflies, damselflies)
   3) Plecoptera (stoneflies)
Additional
   1) Hemiptera (aphids)
   2) Diptera (housefly)
   3) Orthoptera (grasshopper)
   4) Lepidoptera (bugworm)
   5) Hymenoptera ( honeybees, wasps)
   6) Coleoptera (beetles, weevils)

   12) Write the structure present on the thorax and abdomen/
       Segment name of thorax?
On the thorax are the wings and legs. The thorax has its three segments usually quite
clearly marked
   1) Prothorax (anterior most segment)
   2) Mesothorax (middle)
   3) Metathorax (Posterior)

The basic number of segments in the abdomen is eleven plus the telson which bears
the anus. Each segment of the abdomen consists of a
   1) Dorsal sclerite, the tergum, and a
   2) Ventral sclerite, the sternum,
These joined to one another laterally by a pleural membrane. On the abdomen are
various organs such as the ovipositor, sting, cerci and styli, present in some cases,
absent in others.

   1) Larvae of butterflies and moths are commonly called caterpillars,
   2) Those of beetles are usually called grubs,
   3) Those of flies are called maggots,
   4) Larvae found boring in wood, however, whether they will become moths, beetles
      or other insects, are uniformly called borers.

   2)     Characteristics of Insects/ which characters you identify in
          an insect?
   o Bilaterally symmetrical
   o In the Hexapoda or insects the segments of the body are grouped in three distinct
     sections: 1. Head 2. Thorax 3. Abdomen
   o A pair of antennae is present on the head
   o The six legs(3 pairs) are attached to the thorax
   o The four wings(2 pairs) usually present
   o The animals breathe by air tubes
   o The animal is covered by a Shell like skeleton present outside the body, horny in
     nature.
   o Reproductive organs present near the hinder end of the body.
   3)     Types of Insect Head on the basis of their Positions?
Based on the inclination of long axis of the head and orientation of mouth parts there
are three types of insect heads.
        ❖ Hypognathous (Hypo – Below: Gnathous – Jaw):
 Head perpendicular to longitudinal body axis (mouthparts pointed downward). This
includes insects like ants, locusts and beetles.

Basic collecting can be done by simply catching insects with your hands or a net and putting
them into some type of jar. But, for more serious collecting, additional equipment is needed.
Collecting supplies are somewhat dependent on the groups of insects being searched for and the
time of day they are collected. Supplies needed for day collecting can be quite different than
those used for night collecting. The same idea applies to collecting terrestrial insects versus
aquatic insects, or flying insects versus soil dwelling insects. Indeed, it is difficult, if not
impossible to collect all types of insects by an individual on a single collecting outing. It would
also be impractical to carry the many supplies for all collecting methods by a single person.
Many collectors only collect those insects in groups they work with, so they can handle the
material collected in an efficient manner.

have given a list of many of the collecting supplies and traps used by museum personnel and
students below. There are additional traps and supplies, and different methods used by other
collectors around the world, but this should serve as a starting point anyway. There is some
overlap between supplies used for both day and night collecting; therefore those supplies are
included in the same list below. Supplies for collecting aquatic insects are given after the list of
terrestrial insect collecting supplies. Following the collecting supply lists, a list of different types
of traps used for the collection of insects is given. Some of the supplies are more basic than
others, if not necessary; however, the individual can best decide what is most useful to her or
him. Not everything below is linked to a page, because it is fairly obvious what some of the
supplies are for.

          o Use a sweep net to collect flying insects or those on vegetation.

          o Set traps in the ground to collect crawling pests like ants, beetles, and other ground-dwelling
              insects.
          o Use a container with bait or a preservative solution.
   4. Sticky Traps
          o Place adhesive-coated sheets to capture flying pests like whiteflies or thrips.
          o Positioned near crops or suspected pest activity zones.
   5. Beating Tray Method
          o Shake tree branches or plants over a tray to dislodge pests.
          o Effective for collecting caterpillars, mites, or beetles.
   6. Soil Sampling
          o Collect soil samples to study root-associated pests like nematodes or grubs.
          o Often requires specialized sieving or flotation techniques.
   7. Light Traps
          o Use light sources to attract nocturnal pests like moths or certain beetles.
          o Effective during dusk or nighttime field visits.
   8. Vacuum Collection
          o Employ suction devices to collect small or flying pests directly from plants.
          o Useful for aphids, thrips, or mites.

   1. Morphological Identification
        o Use a stereomicroscope or magnifying lens to examine physical characteristics such as:
              ▪ Body shape
              ▪ Wing structure
              ▪ Antennae type
              ▪ Coloration and patterns

         o Compare specimens to identification keys or reference guides.

         o Use dichotomous or pictorial keys to narrow down the pest's identity based on observable traits.

         o Examine microscopic features such as mouthparts, claws, or setae using a compound
             microscope.
         o Useful for small pests like mites or immature insects.

         o Extract DNA and use PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) to identify pests at the molecular level.

         o Utilize software or online databases like iNaturalist or pest management portals for rapid

         o Consult entomologists or pest management experts for ambiguous cases or rare species.

Insect collection is a source of recreation for many people and may be a hobby for those who are interested
in studying insects. Methods of collection and preservation of insects are the pre-requisite to study the
insects and their various internal and external organs. After collection, it becomes imperative to keep and

the insect collection museum. Let ‘s has a look and do the different types methods of collection, devices

Nature of insect collection
A good Zoological collection should consist of at least four (4) individual representatives of each of the
order of insects. So that the collection comprises the great diversity and it should reflect the different forms
occur in insect fauna in a certain ecosystem.
Places (habitat) of insect collection
Insects are omnipresent and abound anywhere and everywhere. A good place to start collecting insects is a
flowering hedgerow or garden where insects can be found on the different parts of plants like flowers,
leaves and stems. Besides these, we can also probe the small insects in the soil or near the roots of plants,
aquatic insects can be collected in water, ponds, streams, rivers, lakes etc. and even do the indoors collection
year round. They can be collected from- Air (flying insects), Water (dragonflies, mayflies and stoneflies
that hover over water, aquatic insects and sea shore insects), Home (from furniture, boxes, bookshelves
(fleas, bugs, flies, and mosquitoes), flower, fruits and vegetables brought in), Debris and animal dung
(which acts as food source for many insects), and from domestic animals and birds (ecto and endo-
parasites). Catching insects: Aerial insects can be caught during flight or after they have alighted.
By sweeping a net through the air or foliage or by beating the foliage and holding the net below.
    ➢ The aerial/ sweep nets can catch aerial insects.
    ➢ Net forceps, dippers and dredge, can catch aquatic insects.
    ➢ Separator and Berlese funnel can catch soil dwelling insects.
Methods of insect collection
1. Hand picking
This method is suitable for catching the large insects like beetles and grasshoppers. It is very tedious (hard
working) method and not suitable for catching the biting and stinging natured
insects.
2. Aerial net or Butterfly net
It is light in weight, useful for catching active fliers like butterflies, moths, dragonflies, wasp, flies etc. The
net consists of three parts viz., loop or frame; handle and porous muslin clothe bags. The diameter of hoop
and the depth of the bag should be in the proportion of 1:2.

3. Sweep net
It is heavier than the aerial net. It consists of short handle, a large loop and dense cloth bag. This is suitable
for collecting leaf hoppers, grasshoppers and other small insects. The net is swept over vegetation.
4. Beating tray
This method is suitable for collecting crawling insects and those, which rest on branches. A beating tray is
held under a branch, which is then hit sharply with a stick.
5. Aspirator/Potters/Suction tube
It is the device to collect small insects in to glass vials with no damage to the specimens. It is employed to
suck in through a rubber tube small and minute insect that is already collected in the net or sitting on wall
or foliage and on the bark of the tree. Usually itis meant for catching more active insects. To prevent entry
of insect in to mouth, a small cloth piece is kept in between the glass and rubber tube.
6. Berlese (Tullgren) funnel
Soil arthropods can be sorted out by these methods. Debris including soil arthropod scan be collected by
using the light as the source of heat in berlese funnel method.
7. Traps- Trapping is a method of collecting insects in the absence of collector. This is the most common
methods or techniques used by growers in Integrated pest management programme to catch the insects.
There are many different types of traps used for collection of insects. They are pheromone traps or sleeve
traps, fruit fly trap, sticky traps, delta traps, water or Wota traps, pit fall trap, wind pan trap, malaise trap
and light traps.
Pheromone traps
Synthetic sex pheromones are placed in the traps to attract male moths. The rubberized septa containing the
pheromone lure are kept in the traps designed especially for this purpose and used in monitoring, mass
trapping and mating disruption programmes. Sticky tarps, Water pan traps and funnel type models are
available for use in pheromone based insect-pest control programmes.
Yellow sticky traps: Aphids, whiteflies, thrips prefer yellow colour. Yellow colour is painted on tin boxes

Explain and Name the types of four stages insect larvae.
About 75% of all insect species go through the four stages of complete metamorphosis - egg,
larva, pupa, and adult. The larva is a specialized feeding stage that looks very different from the
adult.
1) The Egg:Majority of insects begin their life in fertilized eggs. Egg laying amongst insects
depends on the species it belongs to, for example, cockroaches or mantids lay their eggs in a
bunch attached together that forms the ootheca or egg packet.
2) The Larvae:Insect larvae have several distinct ways of hatching. While caterpillar larvae bite
their way out of the eggs during the hatching process. The insect larva undergoes several stages
of molting where it sheds old cuticles multiple times to get new cuticles. Insect larvae vary in
shape depending on the species, therefore they are divided into five kinds. The caterpillar-like
larvae are eruciform, the maggot-like larvae are vermiform, the wire worm-like larvae are
elateriform, the grub-like larvae are scarabaeiform and the long, elongated larvae are
campodeiform. These larvae then transform into pupa and enter the next stage.

Kingdom: Animalia
Phylum: Arthropods
Class: Insecta
Order: Lepidoptera
Is Cutworms insect or pest:
Pest: Cutworms are plump, smooth caterpillars, of several moth species. They feed on all crop
and pasture plants, damaging them near the ground.
In which crops the Cutworms effects:

Cutworms are general feeders that can attack a wide range of plants. Common vegetables they
like to feed on include asparagus, beans, cabbage and other crucifers, carrots, celery, corn,
lettuce, peas, peppers, potatoes and tomatoes. A few species feed on turfgrass.
In which order the Cutworms belongs?, Why Cutworms belong to this order?
Order: Lepidoptera
Reason:
Lepidoptera comes from the Greek words lepido, which means scale and pteron, which means
wing. Butterflies and moths have four wings covered with tiny scales.
Life cycle of Cutworms.
Four (4) stages: the egg, the larva, the pupa, and the adult.
In which stage of life cycle the Cutworms considered as a pest?
larval stage:
The larval stage of various cutworm species (including redbacked, pale western, darksided and
dingy), can cause damage to canola plants by feeding on the cotyledons, leaves, stems or under
soil surfaces.
Biological control of Cutworms in the crops:
Natural enemies of cutworms include predaceous or parasitic insects, mammals, parasitic
nematodes, pathogens, birds, and reptiles. The hymenopteran (wasp) parasites, including
ichneumonids, chalcids, braconids, and sphecids, are the most important group of cutworm
natural enemies.
Chemical method to control Cutworms
We recommended Aerosol/ spraying method to do this.

lambda-cyhalothrin will work very well to reduce damage from cutworms. Safe alternative
products include Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) and insect parasitic nematodes.

                             SHORT QUESTIONS(3)
   1)    Name the parts of legs in insects?
Legs of insects (adults and larvae) are jointed and have five parts:
   1) coxa,
   2) trochanter,
   3) femur,
   4) tibia, and
   5) tarsus.
   2)    Name the part of head of insects/Structures of head?
Structures found on the head are
   1) A pair of antennae
   2) Two compound eyes (ocelli)
   3) The mouth parts

   3)    Define Cerci?
A pair of many-segmented, antenna-like structures, sometimes short, sometimes long,
may occur at the end of the abdomen. And these are called cerci. They probably serve
as organs of touch and possibly organ of smell in some cases.
   4)    What is coxa in insects?
The coxa is the segment that articulates with the body, frequently partly lying in a more
or less cup shaped hollow of the latter. It may be short or long and is generally freely
movable on the body and powerful. This arrangement allows for movement and
flexibility.
   5)    What are tracheal gills?
Insects that live in water during their early stages of life cannot breathe air into their
bodies through spiracles like they do when they are on land. Instead, they have special
structures called tracheal gills that allow them to obtain oxygen from the water. These
tracheal gills help them breathe while they’re in the water.
   6)    What is meant by contact insecticides?
It was formerly supposed that certain materials called contact insecticides, which kill
insects by contact with their bodies. They caused death by entering the spiracles and
closing them up, thus producing suffocation.
   7)    Define Ovipositor?
The ovipositor is a combination of different parts at the end of the abdomen in female
insects that lay their eggs inside objects. It helps them make a hole or slit in the object
and guide the eggs into it. It usually consists of about three pairs of parts, which can be
long or short, slender or stout, depending on the insect. In some insects, the ovipositor
has transformed into a sting because they no longer need to make holes for egg laying.
   8)    How skeleton is formed in Arthropoda?

In arthropods, the skeleton is formed by a process called ecdysis or molting. When an
arthropod grows, its exoskeleton becomes too small and rigid. To accommodate
growth, the arthropod sheds its old exoskeleton and forms a new one. This process
allows them to renew and replace their skeleton as they continue to grow. The surface
of the body is covered by a secretion which hardens on exposure to the air, forming an
outside new shell or external skeleton called exoskeleton.

certain insects.

insects.
Empodium: Between the pulvilli there is often a spine that is called the empodium.

       Molluska/How form exoskeleton of insects?
Both mollusks and arthropods have an external skeleton, which gives them a shell-like
appearance. However, the materials that make up their skeletons are different.
   • Mollusks have a skeleton made mostly of calcium carbonate. e.g. snails.
   • While arthropods have a skeleton made of chitin, which is similar to horn.
     Sometimes, arthropods also have calcareous salts deposited in their chitin. e.g.
     spiders and insects.

absent in others.
